passage:
Text 1
When sea otters returned to an estuary in California, the eelgrass beds there recovered. Otters eat crabs, which eat sea slugs; with fewer crabs, more slugs survived to graze algae off the eelgrass, letting it thrive.

Text 2
Ecologists studying a different estuary found that eelgrass recovered after nutrient pollution from farms was reduced, even though no otters were present. Excess nutrients had fed algae that smothered the grass.
stem: Based on the texts, what would the ecologists in Text 2 most likely say about the findings in Text 1?
choices: The otters' effect on eelgrass may be real, but reducing nutrient pollution can also lead to recovery.
The otters in Text 1 could not have affected eelgrass, since otters are absent from healthy estuaries.
The recovery in Text 1 must have been caused by reduced nutrient pollution rather than otters.
Sea slugs harm eelgrass by eating it directly, which the researchers in Text 1 overlooked.
steps: Both texts link eelgrass recovery to less algae, by different routes (otters vs less pollution).
Text 2's finding shows another route without contradicting Text 1.
Calling the otter effect impossible or insisting pollution must explain Text 1 overstates the case; slugs eat algae, not grass.
key: Two findings can both be true; avoid answers that turn “also” into “instead.”
